traps.trap: Psoas and obturator manoeuvres are swapped

probes.stem_idea: Which manoeuvre elicits the psoas sign? (shared with TR3)
probes.correct: Extension of the right hip with the patient on the left side
distractor_set: Internal rotation of the flexed right hip
Pressure over the left iliac fossa
probes.note: match option length and grammar; every option is a movement or pressure applied by the examiner

probes.stem_idea: Examiner flexes the right hip and rotates the leg inwards; patient winces with hypogastric pain. Name the sign.
probes.correct: Obturator sign
probes.note: retest asks name-from-manoeuvre, the reverse direction of probe 1

traps.diagnoses: Learner remembers that both are right-hip manoeuvres but has not attached each name to its movement.
traps.first_wrong_step: Files 'hip manoeuvre' as one idea, then assigns the movements to the names by feel.

repair.strategy: E1: side-by-side contrast; anchor the movement to the muscle it stretches or the muscle it touches

traps.retest: vignette naming the sign from the manoeuvre; returns inside the TR2 position probe
traps.report_hint: Avoided: sign-to-manoeuvre mapping is secure. Recovered: the two names now sit on the right movements, keep the contrast card. Open: you swap psoas and obturator; rehearse by the movement, not the name.

traps.trap: Each sign is tied to the wrong appendix position

probes.stem_idea: Young man with loin pain, pain on hip extension, little anterior tenderness. Which pairing of sign and appendix position is right?
probes.correct: Psoas sign with retrocaecal; obturator sign with pelvic
distractor_set: Psoas sign with pelvic; obturator sign with retrocaecal
Psoas sign with retrocaecal; right rectal tenderness with retrocaecal
probes.note: options are pairs of equal length; second distractor keeps psoas right so it isolates the rectal-tenderness slip

probes.stem_idea: Why does a pelvic appendix cause diarrhoea, frequency and right rectal tenderness?
probes.correct: It lies against the rectum and bladder, irritating them
distractor_set: It lies on the psoas muscle, stretching it
It lies behind the caecum, irritating the ureter
probes.note: tests position-to-organ contact rather than a memorised pair

traps.diagnoses: Learner stores sign and position as a pair but attaches the pair to the wrong one of the two commonest positions.
traps.first_wrong_step: Memorises 'psoas' and 'pelvic' as a pair without asking which organ the appendix is touching.

repair.strategy: E10: pair recall rebuilt from anatomy (psoas lies behind, rectum and bladder lie in the pelvis); contrast with the position it really belongs to

traps.retest: later sign-matching vignette with a named position in the options; mechanism form above
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you link signs to positions through the organ they touch. Recovered: the pairs now follow the anatomy. Open: you attach signs to the wrong position; redraw the appendix behind and below the caecum.

traps.trap: Rovsing's sign is reversed

probes.stem_idea: Shared with TR1 probe 1: the examiner presses the left iliac fossa and asks where it hurts.
probes.correct: (see TR1 probe 1; Rovsing appears as a distractor there)
probes.note: first surfacing is the TR1 probe-1 distractor; this entry exists so the second probe is a dedicated one

probes.stem_idea: Which statement about Rovsing's sign is correct?
probes.correct: Pressure in the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right iliac fossa
distractor_set: Pressure in the right iliac fossa causes pain in the left iliac fossa
Pain in the right iliac fossa on extension of the right hip
probes.note: tests direction (predict-then-show: where would pressure displace gas?)

traps.diagnoses: Learner runs the sign backwards, putting the pressure where the pain is.
traps.first_wrong_step: Remembers 'pain in RIF' and sets the palpation site to match the pain site.

repair.strategy: E3: predict-then-show; trace the sign: press LIF, colonic gas is pushed towards the caecum, and the inflamed RIF hurts

traps.retest: contrast probe above; also in the end sign-matching vignette
traps.report_hint: Avoided: direction of Rovsing's sign is secure. Recovered: you now press LIF and expect RIF pain. Open: you reverse the direction; narrate the manoeuvre as 'press here, hurts there'.

traps.trap: Pain pathway and causal chain are reversed (RIF first then umbilical; ischaemia before obstruction)

probes.stem_idea: A 19-year-old describes the course of his pain over 12 hours. Which course is typical?
probes.correct: Periumbilical colicky pain that later shifts to the right iliac fossa
distractor_set: Right iliac fossa pain that later spreads to the umbilicus
Constant right iliac fossa pain from the start that never moves
probes.note: both distractors drop the visceral-to-somatic step

probes.stem_idea: Why does the pain localise to the right iliac fossa later?
probes.correct: Inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, giving somatic localised pain
distractor_set: Rising pressure in the lumen stimulates T10 afferents more strongly
Ischaemia of the appendix wall starts before the lumen is blocked
probes.note: second distractor carries the merged TR20 chain reversal

probes.stem_idea: Order the events: obstruction, rising pressure, venous congestion, arterial compromise, gangrene, perforation. Pick the correct order.
probes.correct: Obstruction, rising pressure, venous congestion, arterial compromise, gangrene, perforation
distractor_set: Arterial compromise, obstruction, rising pressure, venous congestion, gangrene, perforation
Obstruction, arterial compromise, rising pressure, gangrene, venous congestion, perforation
probes.note: end-artery fact K4 is the reason gangrene follows quickly; cold probe, no hint

traps.diagnoses: Learner reads the disease from its end-point backwards instead of tracing cause to effect.
traps.first_wrong_step: Starts from the memorised end picture (localised RIF tenderness, gangrene) and places it first.

repair.strategy: E3: predict-then-show; the learner predicts what the T10 visceral supply can and cannot localise, then the chain is traced step by step

traps.retest: mechanism probe in the pathophysiology segment, sequence probe in the cold final segment
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you trace appendicitis from cause to effect. Recovered: the chain now runs obstruction first. Open: you reason from the end-point backwards; say the steps aloud in order.

traps.trap: Symptom order reversed (vomiting before pain)

probes.stem_idea: Murphy's sequence in typical appendicitis.
probes.correct: Pain, then vomiting, then fever
probes.note: sequence is a list with an order, so option lengths are identical

probes.stem_idea: A young adult vomited several times through the morning, then developed diffuse abdominal pain and loose stools. Which reading fits?
probes.correct: Gastroenteritis is more likely, as vomiting preceded the pain
distractor_set: Acute appendicitis, as vomiting is the typical first symptom
Acute appendicitis, as fever and vomiting precede pain early
probes.note: ties the order to its discriminating use

traps.diagnoses: Learner memorised the symptoms as an unordered list, so order carries no meaning.
traps.first_wrong_step: Treats vomiting as an opening symptom because it is the first thing seen in gastroenteritis and obstruction.

repair.strategy: E9: order the steps and ask why pain-first points to a localised process

traps.retest: vignette using the order as the discriminator
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you use symptom order as a clue. Recovered: pain first now anchors your reading. Open: you drop the order; use pain-first as a quick filter against gastroenteritis.

traps.trap: Alvarado weighting and cut-offs are misremembered (migration or rebound scored 2; score read as diagnostic)

probes.stem_idea: Which items score 2 points in the Alvarado score?
probes.correct: Tenderness in the right iliac fossa and leucocytosis
distractor_set: Migration of pain and rebound tenderness
Tenderness in the right iliac fossa and rebound tenderness
probes.note: second distractor keeps one right item, as the brief says learners often recall only one

probes.stem_idea: Patient with migration, nausea, RIF tenderness, rebound and leucocytosis. Compute the Alvarado total.
probes.note: 9 follows from scoring migration and rebound as 2; 6 from scoring leucocytosis as 1; keep options close to avoid a giveaway; offer a number-free variant if the key tends to be the median

probes.stem_idea: What does an Alvarado score of 7 or more mean?
probes.correct: Appendicitis is likely, a risk estimate rather than a test result
distractor_set: Appendicitis is confirmed and imaging can be skipped
Appendicitis is unlikely and the patient can go home
probes.note: carries the merged TR7 cut-off misreading; answer sits in cold final segment

traps.diagnoses: Learner gives the weights to the signs that feel most specific, and reads a risk score as a test result.
traps.first_wrong_step: Assigns the higher weight by how specific the sign feels, not by the scoring table.

repair.strategy: E6: anchor the number to something meaningful (two items weighted 2, total 10) and retest in arithmetic form

traps.retest: arithmetic vignette, then interpretation stem in the cold segment
traps.report_hint: Avoided: the 2-point items and the 7 cut-off are secure. Recovered: tenderness and leucocytosis now carry the 2s. Open: you weigh by how specific a sign feels; rebuild the score from the table.

traps.trap: A negative ultrasound excludes appendicitis in an adult

probes.stem_idea: Adult man, persisting RIF tenderness and rising count; ultrasound could not show the appendix. Next step?
probes.correct: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen
distractor_set: Discharge, as ultrasound has excluded appendicitis
Repeat ultrasound after 6 hours and observe without other imaging
probes.note: an inconclusive scan is not a negative one; keep the stem free of pregnancy or child qualifiers

probes.stem_idea: Which statement about ultrasound in suspected appendicitis in adults is correct?
probes.correct: A negative scan does not exclude it; CT is more accurate
distractor_set: A normal graded-compression scan rules it out
Ultrasound is the most accurate test in adults
probes.note: second distractor is TR11 so the two imaging traps stay separable

traps.diagnoses: Learner treats the first-line test as the decisive test, so a negative result ends the work-up.
traps.first_wrong_step: Carries over 'ultrasound is the first test' as 'ultrasound is the final word'.

repair.strategy: E8: ladder of tests with what each answers; first-line is not confirmatory

traps.retest: recognition form above, then inside the imaging-ladder consolidation
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you know ultrasound is first, not final, in adults. Recovered: a negative scan now triggers a next step. Open: you stop at a negative ultrasound; add CECT to your adult ladder.

traps.trap: CT is used as the first test in children and pregnant women

probes.stem_idea: A 6-year-old with RIF pain, fever and tenderness; which first imaging?
probes.correct: Graded-compression ultrasound
probes.note: qualifier is the age; no other distractor type

probes.stem_idea: Which patient is the one in whom contrast-enhanced CT is the first-choice test? Options differ by patient, not by test.
probes.correct: A 35-year-old man with equivocal signs
distractor_set: A pregnant woman at 26 weeks with RIF pain
probes.note: forces the qualifier to be read

traps.diagnoses: Learner drops the age and setting qualifier and applies the adult answer to every patient.
traps.first_wrong_step: Reads 'CT is most accurate' without checking who the patient is.

repair.strategy: E7: highlight the qualifier; contrast the three patient groups side by side

traps.retest: contrast form by patient; again in the imaging-ladder sequence probe
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you read the patient before choosing the test. Recovered: age and pregnancy now change your first test. Open: you apply the adult CT answer to children and pregnancy; ask 'who is the patient' first.

traps.trap: MRI is chosen as the first-line test in pregnancy

probes.stem_idea: Pregnant woman at 20 weeks with RIF pain; which imaging first?
probes.correct: Graded-compression ultrasound
probes.note: one distractor per trap; shared first probe with TR9

probes.stem_idea: Order the pathway in a pregnant woman with suspected appendicitis.
probes.correct: Ultrasound, then MRI if inconclusive, then surgery as indicated
distractor_set: MRI first, then ultrasound if inconclusive, then surgery
CT first, then MRI if inconclusive, then surgery
probes.note: retest in a different form; teaches the second rung, not just the first

traps.diagnoses: Learner ranks tests by accuracy alone and promotes the best non-ionising test to first place.
traps.first_wrong_step: Picks the most accurate safe test instead of the first rung of the ladder.

repair.strategy: E8: ladder of tests; first rung is cheap, safe and available, MRI is the second rung

traps.retest: sequence probe later; ladder reappears in the cold final segment
traps.report_hint: Avoided: your pregnancy ladder runs ultrasound then MRI. Recovered: MRI is now your second rung. Open: you put MRI first; accuracy is not the only criterion for the first test.

traps.trap: The old PYQ key (ultrasound as investigation of choice in general) is applied to adults

probes.stem_idea: Investigation of choice (most accurate) for acute appendicitis in adults, no other qualifier.
probes.correct: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen
probes.note: MRI is accurate but not the standard answer here, so it is correct-adjacent

probes.stem_idea: Teach both: how should you answer an 'investigation of choice' stem with no age, and what does current practice say?
probes.correct: Read the stem for 'first' or 'most accurate'; older keys favoured ultrasound, current practice CECT in adults
distractor_set: Always answer ultrasound, as PYQs and practice agree
Always answer CT, as ultrasound is now obsolete
probes.note: second distractor is the over-correction; it sits with TR9 because it drops the child and pregnancy qualifier

traps.diagnoses: Learner answers from the keyed past-paper wording without checking what current practice says.
traps.first_wrong_step: Treats a remembered PYQ key as the current standard.

repair.strategy: E5: teach both, 'PYQs expected ultrasound; current practice is ultrasound first in children and pregnancy, CECT most accurate in adults'

traps.retest: contrast form above, then a mixed-age 'IOC' stem in the exam-traps segment
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you answer by the qualifier in the stem. Recovered: you can give the old key and the current answer. Open: you default to the past-paper key; keep 'USG first, CECT most accurate' as a pair.

traps.trap: Pregnancy test is skipped before imaging or surgery in a woman of reproductive age

probes.stem_idea: A 24-year-old woman with RIF pain, irregular cycles, no pregnancy test yet. What first?
probes.correct: Urine or serum beta-hCG
probes.note: stem must not state pregnancy, so CT here is the skipped-test error and not TR9

probes.stem_idea: Order the steps in a woman of reproductive age with suspected appendicitis.
probes.correct: Clinical assessment and beta-hCG, then imaging, then surgery
distractor_set: Clinical assessment, then imaging, then beta-hCG before theatre
Clinical assessment, then surgery, then beta-hCG if the appendix is normal
probes.note: tests priority, not the test itself

traps.diagnoses: Learner follows the working diagnosis and treats the pregnancy test as an afterthought.
traps.first_wrong_step: Starts the diagnostic step for the favoured disease before excluding the one that changes everything.

repair.strategy: E9: order the steps; ask 'what first, and why' (ectopic pregnancy changes both imaging and surgery)

traps.retest: sequence form later in the women's differential segment
traps.report_hint: Avoided: beta-hCG comes first in your plan. Recovered: pregnancy is excluded before imaging. Open: you start with the appendix; in any woman of reproductive age, test pregnancy first.

traps.trap: A different condition is picked as the most common abdominal surgical emergency

probes.stem_idea: Most common surgical emergency of the abdomen?
probes.correct: Acute appendicitis
probes.note: match option length; keep 'Acute' on every option so the key is not the only one with it

probes.stem_idea: Most common non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy?
probes.correct: Acute appendicitis
probes.note: retest in a narrower setting; the qualifier changes the pool but not the answer

traps.diagnoses: Learner reads 'most common' as 'most dangerous' or 'most often tested'.
traps.first_wrong_step: Substitutes severity for frequency.

repair.strategy: E4: show the exact qualifier 'most common'; counter-case: perforated ulcer kills more but occurs less

traps.retest: contrast form in the pregnancy segment
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you read 'most common' as frequency. Recovered: appendicitis tops the list by frequency. Open: you equate common with serious; read the qualifier word first.

traps.trap: RIF pain always means appendicitis

probes.stem_idea: Young woman, sudden mid-cycle RIF pain, no migration, afebrile, normal count, settles over hours. Most likely diagnosis?
probes.correct: Mittelschmerz
probes.note: PID is a true differential in women but fits the stem less

probes.stem_idea: 68-year-old man, RIF mass, anaemia, change in bowel habit. Most likely diagnosis?
probes.correct: Caecal carcinoma
probes.note: sigmoid diverticulitis is a true elderly differential, but is left-sided

traps.diagnoses: Learner stops generalising at the textbook case and drops the differential for each age group.
traps.first_wrong_step: Treats the classic pattern as the only pattern.

repair.strategy: E4: counter-case by group (child, woman, elderly) with the discriminating feature in each

traps.retest: second vignette in a different age group
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you build a differential by age and sex. Recovered: you can name what mimics appendicitis. Open: you default to appendicitis; list three look-alikes for each group.

traps.trap: Obstruction cause is age-blind (faecolith in the child, lymphoid hyperplasia in the adult)

probes.stem_idea: An 8-year-old with a recent viral illness and RIF pain; commonest cause of luminal obstruction?
probes.correct: Lymphoid hyperplasia
probes.note: worms are a true but less common cause, so correct-adjacent

probes.stem_idea: A 45-year-old whose CT shows an appendicolith; commonest cause of obstruction in this age group?
probes.correct: Faecolith
probes.note: same options swapped; the age in the stem is the only discriminator

traps.diagnoses: Learner ignores the age in the stem and picks the more familiar cause.
traps.first_wrong_step: Does not check which cause predominates in the age group asked.

repair.strategy: E7: highlight the qualifier; contrast the two settings through the lymphoid tissue that atrophies with age

traps.retest: mirror stem with the age reversed
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you check the age before the cause. Recovered: lymphoid in the young, faecolith in adults. Open: you ignore the age; link cause to the lymphoid tissue available.

traps.trap: Disease complications are merged with complications of appendicectomy

probes.stem_idea: Which of the following is a complication of appendicectomy?
probes.correct: Faecal fistula
probes.note: disease complications offered as surgical ones

probes.stem_idea: Which is NOT a complication of acute appendicitis itself (before surgery)?
probes.correct: Stump appendicitis
probes.note: true disease complications; choosing one shows the merged list

probes.stem_idea: Most common complication after appendicectomy (merged TR17: qualifier drop).
probes.correct: Wound infection
probes.note: faecal fistula is a true surgical complication but rare; cold probe, no hint

traps.diagnoses: Learner merges the two complication lists from the same chapter into one.
traps.first_wrong_step: Does not ask whether the complication arises from the disease or from the operation.

repair.strategy: E2: rebuild the two sets from their logic (disease: perforation, mass, abscess, pylephlebitis; operation: wound infection, fistula, stump, hernia); which-is-not retest

traps.retest: which-is-not probe plus a cold 'most common' probe
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you keep disease and operation complications apart. Recovered: the two lists are rebuilt. Open: you merge the lists; ask 'from the disease or from the knife' for each item.

traps.trap: Nerve injured by a gridiron incision is named wrongly

probes.stem_idea: Nerve injured by a gridiron incision leading to right inguinal hernia?
probes.correct: Ilioinguinal nerve
probes.note: three neighbouring nerves of the iliac region

probes.stem_idea: A 28-year-old develops a right groin bulge and numbness over the groin after open appendicectomy through McBurney's point. Which nerve was injured?
probes.correct: Ilioinguinal nerve
probes.note: options reordered from probe 1; key must not repeat its slot

traps.diagnoses: Learner has learned the iliac-region nerves as a bundle and cannot tell which crosses the incision.
traps.first_wrong_step: Attaches the incision to its neighbour nerve because the three are learned together.

repair.strategy: E10: pair recall; contrast the nerve with the neighbours it is confused with, tied to the gridiron's oblique muscle split

traps.retest: vignette form with a different surface
traps.report_hint: Avoided: the incision and ilioinguinal nerve are paired in your memory. Recovered: you now pair them. Open: you confuse neighbouring nerves; draw the three nerves on the gridiron site.

traps.trap: Appendicectomy is the only treatment for appendicitis

probes.stem_idea: A motivated adult with CT-proven uncomplicated appendicitis; which statement is correct?
probes.correct: Antibiotics-first is an accepted option for selected patients
distractor_set: Antibiotics alone are never acceptable in appendicitis
Antibiotics-first is now the preferred treatment for all appendicitis
probes.note: second distractor is the over-correction and sits with TR23

probes.stem_idea: Teach both: how to answer 'treatment of choice' and 'only treatment' stems.
probes.correct: Treatment of choice is appendicectomy; 'only treatment' is the older key, practice allows selected antibiotics-first
distractor_set: Appendicectomy is the only treatment, with no non-operative option
Antibiotics have replaced appendicectomy as the treatment of choice
probes.note: key is not shorter or longer than the options

traps.diagnoses: Learner holds a past-paper absolute that current practice has softened.
traps.first_wrong_step: Takes 'treatment of choice' as 'only treatment'.

repair.strategy: E5: teach both, 'PYQs expected X; current practice is Y'

traps.retest: contrast form later in the exam-traps segment
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you separate exam key from practice. Recovered: you can state both. Open: you hold the old absolute; add antibiotics-first for selected uncomplicated cases to your notes.

traps.trap: Antibiotics-first is offered to a patient with an appendicolith or complicated disease

probes.stem_idea: 34-year-old, CT-proven appendicitis with an appendicolith. Best management?
probes.correct: Appendicectomy, as the appendicolith predicts failure of antibiotics
distractor_set: Antibiotics alone, as the CT shows no perforation
Ochsner-Sherren regimen, as for an appendicular mass
probes.note: second distractor is a conservative-regimen conflation owned by TR25

probes.stem_idea: Which patient is the best candidate for antibiotics-first treatment?
probes.correct: Adult with CT-proven uncomplicated disease and no appendicolith
distractor_set: Adult with CT-proven disease and an appendicolith
Adult with perforation and a localised collection
probes.note: options differ only in the qualifier

traps.diagnoses: Learner keeps 'antibiotics-first is acceptable' and drops the three qualifiers.
traps.first_wrong_step: Stores the headline option without its conditions.

repair.strategy: E7: highlight the qualifier; contrast uncomplicated with complicated

traps.retest: contrast form by patient
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you check the qualifiers before offering antibiotics-first. Recovered: you now name uncomplicated, CT-proven, no appendicolith. Open: you drop the qualifiers; review the three conditions.

traps.trap: Interval appendicectomy at 6-8 weeks is applied routinely after an appendicular mass

probes.stem_idea: After successful conservative treatment of an appendicular mass, what is the traditional teaching and the current view?
probes.correct: Traditionally interval surgery at 6-8 weeks, now selective with colonoscopy or CT in older patients
distractor_set: Routine interval appendicectomy at 6-8 weeks in every patient
No interval surgery or further work-up is ever needed
probes.note: second distractor is the over-correction of the same key

probes.stem_idea: A 55-year-old man whose mass has resolved on the regimen. Next step?
probes.correct: Colonoscopy or CT to exclude caecal carcinoma, then selective interval surgery
distractor_set: Routine interval appendicectomy at 6-8 weeks with no other work-up
probes.note: age is the qualifier that drives the work-up

traps.diagnoses: Learner applies the keyed interval operation as routine without the current selective approach.
traps.first_wrong_step: Treats the old key as fixed policy and skips the malignancy check.

repair.strategy: E5: teach both, 'PYQs expected routine interval surgery at 6-8 weeks; current practice is selective, with work-up in older patients'

traps.retest: vignette with an older patient
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you give the key and the modern view. Recovered: selective surgery with work-up is clear. Open: you apply interval surgery to everyone; remember the older-patient work-up.

traps.trap: Immediate surgery for an appendicular mass or open drainage for an abscess

probes.stem_idea: Five days of RIF pain, now a tender palpable mass, stable, low-grade fever. Next step?
probes.correct: Conservative management by the Ochsner-Sherren regimen
probes.note: stem states a mass, not an abscess or peritonitis

probes.stem_idea: Swinging fever, imaging shows a drainable appendicular collection. Best treatment?
probes.correct: Image-guided percutaneous drainage with antibiotics
probes.note: options reorder from probe 1; folds in the merged TR26 first-step error

traps.diagnoses: Learner jumps to surgery at once and skips the conservative or image-guided first step.
traps.first_wrong_step: Reads 'appendicitis means appendicectomy' as 'always operate now'.

repair.strategy: E9: order the steps; ask what first and why; trace when the regimen is stopped

traps.retest: abscess vignette in a different form
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you pick the first step for mass and abscess. Recovered: conservative for a mass, percutaneous for an abscess. Open: you operate first; learn the sequence.

merged into TR25 (open drainage first is probe 2 of TR25)

dropped, medium yield; pregnancy surgery timing, lower exam frequency

dropped, medium yield; retrocaecal presentation covered inside TR2 repair
dropped, medium yield; retrocaecal look-alike covered by TR14 differential

probe_plan: Backbone traps are TR4 (visceral-to-somatic pain and the obstruction-first chain, which every later clinical stem builds on), TR1 and TR2 (sign, manoeuvre and position, one wrong model of 'hip signs'), the imaging ladder TR8, TR9, TR10 and TR11 (one shared first-rung idea with patient qualifiers), TR25, TR24 and TR22 (the management ladder from mass to abscess to antibiotics-first), and TR16 (two complication lists). Meet them in this order. Hook and definition segment: TR13 (most common), TR15. Mechanism segment: TR4 probes 1 and 2, TR5. Clinical-picture segment: TR1 with TR3 on one shared probe, then TR2, TR6 probes 1 and 2, TR14 probe 1. Investigation segment: TR12 probe 1, TR9 and TR10 on a shared pregnancy probe, TR8, TR11. Management segment: TR25, TR24, TR22, TR23. Complications and exam-traps segment: TR16 probe 1, TR18, TR14 probe 2, TR13 probe 2. Cold final segment (no hints): TR4 sequence, TR6 interpretation, TR16 'most common', TR10 sequence, TR12 sequence. Shared stems are TR1 with TR3, TR9 with TR10, and TR22 with TR23, each with one option per trap. Over-correction options (for example 'always CT', 'antibiotics replace surgery') are assigned to the trap whose qualifier they drop, not to the PYQ-key trap they reject.
